learn: The principles of design describe how artists organise elements: balance, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, proportion, unity and variety.
Radial balance radiates from a centre, like a rose window.
Proportion is the size relationship of parts to each other and the whole.
check: Proportion is the size relationship of...
Which is a principle of design?
lessons.try: Create a radial design inside a circle.

learn: Emphasis creates a focal point using contrast, isolation, placement or convergence (lines pointing to it).
Movement leads the viewer's eye through the composition.
Leading lines, like a winding road, guide movement.
check: Lines pointing to a focal point create...
A winding road can act as a...
lessons.try: Draw a composition where lines lead to a focal point.

learn: Unity makes an artwork feel whole and connected.
Variety adds interest through differences.
Great art balances unity and variety: too much unity is boring; too much variety is chaotic.
lessons.try: Make a collage with a unified colour scheme but varied shapes.

learn: Monochromatic: one hue in tints and shades. Analogous: neighbours on the wheel. Complementary: opposites.
Triadic: three evenly spaced hues. Split-complementary: one hue plus the two next to its complement.
Warm and cool schemes set temperature and mood.
check: One hue plus the two next to its complement is...
lessons.try: Make a mini colour-scheme reference card for each scheme.

learn: Colours change in different light: warm sunset light makes things orange; shade makes them bluish.
Impressionists studied how light changes colour.
Shadows often contain the complementary colour of the light.
check: Who studied how light changes colour?
lessons.try: Observe an object at noon and at sunset and note colour changes.

learn: Expressionist artists used non-realistic colour to show emotion.
Franz Marc painted blue horses to express spirituality.
Colour can communicate feelings beyond realism.
lessons.try: Paint an animal in unexpected colours that express a feeling.

learn: In one-point perspective, parallel lines receding from the viewer meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line.
Front faces of objects remain flat rectangles.
Orthogonal lines are the lines that go to the vanishing point.
check: Lines that go to the vanishing point are...
Front faces in one-point perspective remain...
The vanishing point sits on the...
lessons.try: Draw a set of boxes floating around a vanishing point.

learn: A one-point room places the vanishing point in the back wall.
Floor, ceiling and side walls angle toward the vanishing point.
Add doors, windows and furniture using orthogonal lines.
check: In a one-point room, the vanishing point is in the...
lessons.try: Draw your bedroom in one-point perspective.

learn: Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective in Florence around 1415.
Leonardo da Vinci's "The Last Supper" uses one-point perspective with the vanishing point behind Jesus' head.
Perspective changed Western art forever.
check: In "The Last Supper", the vanishing point is behind...
lessons.try: Find the vanishing point in a picture of "The Last Supper".

learn: Highlight, midtone, core shadow, reflected light and cast shadow describe light on a form.
A consistent light source makes drawings believable.
Value contrast creates drama.
check: A consistent light source makes drawings...
lessons.try: Shade a cube, cylinder and cone lit from one side.

learn: Chiaroscuro means strong contrast between light and dark.
Caravaggio used dramatic chiaroscuro in the late 1500s and early 1600s.
It creates mood and focus.
lessons.try: Draw a face lit dramatically from one side.

learn: Different textures reflect light differently: shiny metal has sharp highlights; cloth has soft gradations.
Glass shows reflections and transparency.
Observing carefully helps you render textures.
lessons.try: Draw a shiny spoon and a soft towel.

learn: Gesture drawings are quick sketches that capture action and movement.
Start with a "line of action", a curved line showing the main movement.
Work fast: 30 seconds to 2 minutes per pose.
check: The main movement line is the...
lessons.try: Do ten 1-minute gesture drawings of people in videos or at a park.

learn: Adults are about 7 to 8 heads tall.
The halfway point is at the hips.
Knees are about a quarter of the way up from the feet.
check: Adults are about how many heads tall?
The halfway point of the body is at the...
Knees are about ___ up from the feet.
lessons.try: Draw a figure using head-height measurements.

learn: Show weight shift: in a standing pose, hips and shoulders tilt opposite ways (contrapposto).
Use foreshortening for limbs coming toward the viewer.
Clothing folds follow the body's movement.
check: Hips and shoulders tilting opposite ways is...
Limbs coming toward the viewer use...
lessons.try: Draw a friend in a sports pose.

learn: Impressionism began in France in the 1870s.
Artists painted outdoors (en plein air) to capture light and atmosphere.
They used visible, quick brushstrokes and bright colours.
lessons.try: Paint outdoors for 20 minutes, capturing the light.

learn: Claude Monet's "Impression, Sunrise" (1872) gave the movement its name.
Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted joyful scenes of people.
Mary Cassatt, an American, painted mothers and children; Edgar Degas painted dancers.
lessons.try: Compare a Monet landscape and a Degas dancer painting.

learn: Post-Impressionists built on Impressionism with stronger structure or emotion.
Vincent van Gogh used thick swirling paint; Georges Seurat used dots of colour (pointillism).
Paul Cézanne simplified forms into geometric shapes.
check: Who simplified forms into geometric shapes?
lessons.try: Make a small pointillist picture with marker dots.

learn: Abstract art doesn't try to look exactly like real things.
It may simplify real objects or use only shapes, lines and colours.
Abstract art expresses ideas and feelings through elements and principles.
check: Doesn't try to look exactly real
lessons.try: Make an abstract drawing of a sound you like.

learn: Wassily Kandinsky painted some of the first fully abstract works around 1910, linking colours to music.
Piet Mondrian used grids of black lines with red, yellow and blue rectangles.
Georgia O'Keeffe painted enlarged flowers that border on abstraction.
lessons.try: Create a Mondrian-style grid composition.

learn: Cubism, by Picasso and Braque, showed subjects from multiple viewpoints at once.
Surrealism, in the 1920s, painted dreamlike scenes, like Salvador Dalí's melting clocks.
Modern art movements broke traditional rules.
lessons.try: Draw an object from three angles combined into one image.

learn: Assemblage is 3D art made from found objects.
Artists combine everyday items to create new meanings.
Joseph Cornell made famous shadow boxes filled with small objects.
lessons.try: Make a shadow box about yourself using small found objects.

learn: Relief sculpture projects from a background: low relief (bas-relief) barely projects; high relief projects far.
Carving removes material (subtractive).
Coins, building friezes and monuments use relief.
lessons.try: Carve a low relief design into a soft material like a foam block.

learn: Kinetic sculpture moves.
Alexander Calder invented the mobile in the 1930s, with shapes balanced on wires.
Balance is key: each side must counterweight the other.
lessons.try: Build a small mobile from wire or sticks and paper shapes.

learn: Graphic design combines text and images to communicate.
Logos, posters, book covers and websites are graphic design.
Good design is clear, readable and eye-catching.
lessons.try: Redesign the cover of a favourite book.

learn: Typography is the art of arranging letters.
Serif fonts have small strokes at the ends of letters; sans-serif fonts don't.
Size, weight and spacing create hierarchy, showing what to read first.
check: Typography is the art of arranging...
lessons.try: Hand-letter your name in a serif and a sans-serif style.

learn: A logo is a simple symbol representing a company or group.
Strong logos are simple, memorable and work in black and white.
Symbols communicate quickly without words, like road signs.
lessons.try: Design a logo for a club you'd like to start.

learn: Constructive feedback is specific and kind: "The colours in the sky create a calm mood" rather than "It's nice."
Use a "glow and grow": one strength and one suggestion.
Receive feedback openly; it helps you improve.
check: A "glow and grow" includes a strength and a...
lessons.try: Give a "glow and grow" on a classmate's or family member's art.

learn: A portfolio is a collection of your best artwork.
Include variety: different media, subjects and techniques.
Label each piece with title, medium, date and a short reflection.
check: A portfolio is a collection of your...
Each piece should be labelled with...
lessons.try: Choose your five best artworks this year for a portfolio.

learn: Compare early and recent work to see your growth.
Write about challenges you overcame and skills you learned.
Set goals for what you want to learn next.
check: Comparing early and recent work shows your...
lessons.try: Write a one-page reflection on your growth as an artist.
